title: Apollo 13 Imax Format
full_review:
The Academy Award-winning "Apollo 13" (Universal) hit the big screen in 1995, but now it's coming back on a really big screen.

This rerelease marks the first time a live-action motion picture has been converted from standard 35 mm format to the digitally remastered 70 mm Imax format. Imax screens in over 100 theaters across the country project visuals up to eight stories high for exceptional detail and clarity of image.

But since Imax projectors can only accommodate movies no longer than two hours, director Ron Howard had to trim about 20 minutes from his original film. Happily, the cuts included a few mild cuss words, a slightly risque shot of a woman in the shower and an off-duty astronaut getting tipsy. Otherwise, it's the same movie, only a lot larger.

"Apollo 13" was a good choice for the first Hollywood movie to go Imax as the space vistas are even more impressive in the magnified format and some of the close-ups are startling. The panning shots, however, exaggerate the momentary blurriness on screen while the camera is moving.

"Apollo 13" is a wonderful movie and after a few minutes you actually forget about the size and scope of the images as the story takes hold. And that is the challenge for the Imax people : If they remaster a fine film it's all to the good, but a poorly written, acted or directed movie won't play any better simply by virtue of its improved technology.

The original review of the 1995 film follows:

The prognosis looked grim back in April 1970 when three American astronauts in space were ordered to abort a moon landing and instead attempt to return to Earth on diminishing supplies of oxygen and electrical power. Such is the dramatic true story of "Apollo 13" from director Ron Howard and Universal Pictures.

Veteran astronaut Jim Lovell (Tom Hanks) is delighted when his moon mission comes up ahead of schedule and practice sessions with fellow co-pilots Ken Mattingly (Gary Sinise) and Fred Haise (Bill Paxton) demonstrate solid teamwork.

However, when measles-exposed Mattingly is scrubbed at the 11th hour, less experienced Jack Swigert (Kevin Bacon) steps in. Dismissing superstitious warnings that the Apollo mission was number 13, taking off at 13:13 hours and set to land on the moon on April 13, the trio blasts off. Watching takeoff at Cape Canaveral are Mrs. Lovell (Kathleen Quinlan) and Mrs. Haise (Tracy Reiner), who hide their fears behind fake smiles for the press.

Nearing the moon a smooth 55 hours into the flight a routine procedure backfired, followed by an explosion that crippled the spacecraft. With oxygen leaking out and power and guidance systems compromised, Houston Mission Control flight director Gene Kranz (Ed Harris) canceled the moon landing and directed the engineers, mathematicians and scientists assembled to focus exclusively on getting the three men home alive.

Left back on earth when Apollo13 took off, Mattingly's experience in the simulator suddenly becomes crucial in desperately trying to devise new methods of return and re-entry using the minimal power available.

With temperatures plummeting to freezing, the three are forced to abandon the command module and cram into the lunar module, designed for two people with a two-day supply of oxygen. They are four days from the earth's atmosphere. It is doubtful their power will last that long. Dangerous levels of carbon dioxide are building and there is no precedent on how to safely return the damaged spacecraft under such alarming conditions.

With the focus squarely on the human element, Howard quickly builds on the emotional tensions and keeps the suspense level simmering. This is no mean feat when so much of the action -- or waiting really -- takes place within the tight confines of the tiny module. Cutting from space to the intense search for solutions at mission control to Walter Cronkite updating a tense America, the pacing never lags as even more problems present an ominous picture of insurmountable odds.

Only one aspect of the story is thoroughly predictable and staged flatly: the relationship between the two married astronauts and their worried wives, teary-eyed children in tow.

However, the blastoff and re-entry sequences are spectacularly filmed, heart-stopping, and not only give one a sense of the majesty of space but of the mind-boggling preparations necessary to ensure a successful space mission.

Hanks turns in his accustomed fine performance, keeping his imperiled shipmates on an even keel when the finger-pointing begins and refusing to let either believe that Houston knows they are doomed but won't say so. Harris is also especially good as the barely contained flight director for whom "failure is not an option."

If anything, the movie errs on the side of flag-waving, with all the big and little guys at mission control portrayed as both ingenious and heroic in their round-the-clock efforts to save the astronauts. And the closing narration implies the space program should be a higher priority, unnecessarily politicizing the story, which is based on Lovell and Jeffrey Kluger's book, "Lost Moon."

Lay people may find some of the technical jargon a bit daunting but it never gets in the way of the riveting rescue mission at hand.

With Americans starved for heroes in this cynical age, "Apollo 13" offers a slew of them and its box office is likely to reach and stay at celestial heights for many moons.

Because of fleeting sexual innuendo and minor profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
